title: Introduction to AI and Generative AI
description: What AI actually is, how generative AI differs from everything before it, and where it genuinely helps and genuinely fails.

lessons.title: What artificial intelligence actually is
lessons.description: A working definition of AI, and the three eras that produced today's tools.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Artificial intelligence is software that does things we would normally call thinking: recognising a face, understanding a sentence, spotting a pattern, making a decision.

That definition is deliberately loose, because the field is loose. A spam filter is AI. So is the system that suggests the next word on your phone keyboard. So is a program that plays chess better than any human. They have almost nothing in common technically. What they share is that each one handles a task that used to need a person.

It helps to notice what AI is **not**. It is not a mind. It has no intentions, no understanding of consequences, and no opinion about whether its answer is a good idea. It produces output that fits a pattern. Everything else you might read into it is you, not it.

### A short history, in three steps

Early AI, from the 1950s onward, was **rule-based**. People wrote the rules by hand: if the temperature is above this and the pressure below that, sound the alarm. This works well for problems you can fully describe, and falls apart for problems you cannot. Nobody can write the rules for recognising a cat.

From the 1990s, **machine learning** took over. Instead of writing rules, you show the computer thousands of examples and let it work out the rule itself. Show it enough photos labelled "cat" and "not a cat" and it learns what a cat looks like, without anyone ever defining one.

From around 2012, **deep learning** made this dramatically better by using much larger networks trained on much more data. This is the wave that produced the systems people now call AI in everyday conversation.

## Demonstrate

Think about how a bank decides whether a card transaction is fraudulent.

The rule-based way: block any transaction over a certain amount from a foreign country. Simple, and wrong constantly. It blocks your holiday, and it misses the fraudster who makes forty small purchases at home.

The machine learning way: feed the system millions of past transactions, each labelled fraud or not fraud. It finds patterns no one wrote down, such as a small test purchase followed within minutes by a large one, or a spending pattern that does not match this particular customer. Nobody told it to look for that. It found it in the data.

Notice what changed. In the first approach, a human decided what mattered. In the second, the human decided what the *goal* was, and the machine worked out what mattered.

## Practice

Spend ten minutes on this before moving on.

List five things you did in the last week that involved software making a judgement rather than following an instruction you gave it. Some starting points: a recommended video, a photo search, a route suggestion, an autocorrect, a shopping suggestion, a filtered email.

For each one, write a sentence answering: could a person have written the rule for this by hand? If not, why not?

Keep your list. You will come back to it in the module assignment.

## What to remember

- AI is software doing tasks we would call thinking; it is not a mind
- Rule-based systems need a human to write down what matters
- Machine learning works out what matters from examples
- Deep learning is machine learning at a much larger scale, and is behind most of what people now call AI

lessons.title: AI, machine learning and deep learning
lessons.description: Three terms that nest inside one another, and why the difference changes how systems fail.
lessons.content:
## Learn

These three words get used as if they mean the same thing. They do not. They sit inside one another, like boxes.

**Artificial intelligence** is the whole field: any software doing something we would call intelligent.

**Machine learning** is one approach within AI: the computer learns the rule from examples instead of being given it.

**Deep learning** is one approach within machine learning: it uses neural networks with many layers, and needs a great deal of data and computing power.

So every deep learning system is machine learning, and every machine learning system is AI. The reverse is not true. A chess program from 1990 is AI but not machine learning.

### Why the distinction matters to you

It matters because it tells you what a system can and cannot do.

A rule-based system fails **loudly**. Give it something outside its rules and it produces an error, or nothing. You know it failed.

A machine learning system fails **quietly**. Give it something unlike anything it was trained on and it still produces an answer, confidently, and the answer may be nonsense. Nothing in the output tells you the system is out of its depth.

This single difference explains most of the surprises people have with AI, and we will come back to it in almost every module.

## Demonstrate

Three systems, three approaches.

A **tax calculator** applies rules written by an accountant. The rules come from law. If the law changes, someone edits the rules. It is AI only in the loosest sense, and it is completely predictable.

A **spam filter** is machine learning. It was trained on millions of emails marked spam or not spam. It works out which words, senders and patterns predict spam. When spammers change tactics, the filter can be retrained on new examples. No one rewrites its rules by hand.

**ChatGPT** is deep learning. It is a neural network with a very large number of parameters, trained on an enormous amount of text. Nobody can point to the part of it that knows about cooking, or French, or Python. That knowledge is spread across the whole network.

## Practice

For each of these, decide whether it is best described as rule-based, machine learning, or deep learning, and write one line saying why:

1. A thermostat that turns on heating below 18 degrees
2. A photo app that groups pictures of the same person together
3. A chatbot that answers questions about a company's products in natural language
4. A form that rejects a password shorter than eight characters
5. A system that predicts which customers are likely to cancel a subscription

Then, for the two you labelled machine learning or deep learning, write down one way each could fail quietly.

## What to remember

- The three terms nest: deep learning is inside machine learning, which is inside AI
- Rule-based systems fail loudly, which is inconvenient but honest
- Learned systems fail quietly and confidently, which is the risk you manage throughout this course

lessons.title: What generative AI is
lessons.description: The line between labelling things that exist and producing something new.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Most AI you have used so far **classifies** or **predicts**. It takes something in and gives you a label or a number out. Is this spam or not? Which face is this? How likely is this customer to leave?

Generative AI produces something new. Give it a request and it creates text, an image, audio, video or code that did not exist before.

That is the whole distinction. Traditional AI answers a question about existing things. Generative AI makes a new thing.

### What "new" actually means

This deserves care, because it is where most misunderstandings begin.

A generative model does not copy and paste from a library of stored answers. It learned patterns from an enormous number of examples, and it produces output that fits those patterns. The specific sentence it writes for you has very likely never been written before in that exact form.

But it is also not inventing from nothing, the way a person can have a genuinely new idea. It is producing a highly plausible combination of patterns it has seen. That is why it is brilliant at things that follow a shape, such as a cover letter, a summary, a SQL query, or a product photograph, and much weaker at things that require an idea nobody has had.

### Generative AI versus traditional AI, side by side

- Traditional AI takes an input and returns a **label, number or decision**. Generative AI takes an input and returns **new content**.
- Traditional AI is usually judged on **accuracy** against a known right answer. Generative AI usually has no single right answer, so it is judged on whether the output is **useful, correct and appropriate**.
- Traditional AI usually does **one narrow task** it was trained for. A generative model does a **very wide range of tasks** it was never specifically trained for.

That last point is the surprising one. Nobody trained a language model to write a haiku about a tax return. It can, because writing haikus and writing about tax returns are both patterns in the text it learned from.

## Demonstrate

Take one situation, a customer complaint email, and see both kinds of AI at work.

Traditional AI on that email: classify the sentiment as negative, route it to the complaints team, predict the likelihood this customer cancels. Three useful outputs, each a label or a number.

Generative AI on the same email: summarise it in two lines, draft a reply, rewrite the reply to be warmer, translate it into Hindi, and pull out every specific commitment the company made. Five useful outputs, each new content.

In practice, real products use both. The classifier decides where the email goes. The generative model drafts what to say back.

## Practice

Pick a task you do regularly, at work or in your studies. Write it at the top of a page.

Underneath, write two lists. First, the parts of that task that are **judgements**: decisions, categories, priorities, yes or no. Second, the parts that are **production**: writing, drawing, summarising, formatting, explaining.

The second list is where generative AI will help you in this course. The first list is where you should be careful, and where a human judgement usually still belongs.

## What to remember

- Traditional AI labels and predicts; generative AI produces new content
- Generative output is a plausible new combination of learned patterns, not a copy and not a genuinely new idea
- One generative model can do a very wide range of tasks it was never specifically trained for
- Most real systems combine both kinds

lessons.title: The five kinds of generative AI
lessons.description: Text, images, audio, video and code, and how reliable each one is today.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Generative AI is usually grouped by what it produces. There are five kinds worth knowing, and you will use all of them in this course.

### Text

The most mature and most useful. Writing, rewriting, summarising, translating, answering questions, extracting information from documents, explaining things. This is what large language models do, and modules 2 to 6 are largely about them.

### Images

Produce a picture from a text description, or edit an existing picture. Used for illustration, product mockups, marketing graphics, concept art and design exploration. Module 7 covers this.

### Audio

Two quite different things share this label. **Speech**, where a model reads text aloud in a chosen voice, or clones a voice from a sample. And **music**, where a model composes and performs. Module 8 covers both.

### Video

The newest and least reliable of the five. Produce a short clip from a text description, animate a still image, or generate a presenter who appears to speak. Quality varies enormously and it changes fast. Module 8 covers this too.

### Code

Write a function, explain unfamiliar code, find a bug, write tests, convert from one language to another. This is text generation applied to a very structured kind of text, which is why models are unusually good at it. Modules 9 and 12 cover this.

### Where the lines blur

Increasingly, one model does several of these. A **multimodal** model accepts more than one kind of input, or produces more than one kind of output. You can show it a photograph and ask a question about it in text, or give it text and get an image. Module 3 looks at this properly.

Do not expect the five categories to stay neatly separated. They are a useful way to organise learning, not a description of how products are built.

## Demonstrate

Imagine you are launching a small business and need a product page.

- **Text**: write the product description, the FAQ and the meta description
- **Images**: generate a hero image and three lifestyle shots
- **Audio**: narrate a thirty-second explainer in a voice you choose
- **Video**: turn the still images and narration into a short clip
- **Code**: build the page itself, and a form that sends enquiries to your inbox

Five kinds of generation, one afternoon, one person. That is genuinely new, and it is the reason this course exists.

Be honest about the limits, though. The text will need editing. The images may get hands and text wrong. The video will look like AI video. The code will need testing. None of this is push-button.

## Practice

Choose a small project of your own: a college society event, a side business, a portfolio site, a family newsletter.

Write down, for each of the five kinds, one specific thing you would want generated for that project. Be specific. Not "some images" but "a banner showing a study group at a table, warm lighting, landscape".

Keep this list. Several later modules ask you to actually produce these.

## What to remember

- The five kinds are text, images, audio, video and code
- Text and code are the most reliable today; video is the least
- Multimodal models cross these boundaries, and the boundaries are blurring
- Everything generated needs a human to check it before it is used

lessons.title: Where generative AI is already used
lessons.description: Honest accounts of real deployments, and the question to ask about every AI claim.
lessons.content:
## Learn

It is easy to find breathless claims about AI and hard to find honest accounts of where it is actually earning its place. Here are the areas where generative AI is genuinely in daily use, and what it is really doing in each.

### Writing and communication

Drafting emails, reports, proposals and summaries. The pattern that works is **AI drafts, human edits**, not AI publishes. It is fastest where the format is predictable and the stakes of a first draft are low.

### Customer support

Answering common questions, summarising long conversations for the next agent, drafting replies that a person approves before sending. The successful deployments keep a human in the loop for anything unusual.

### Software development

Generating boilerplate, explaining unfamiliar code, writing tests, suggesting fixes. Surveys consistently find developers report real time savings on routine work, and much less benefit on hard problems.

### Education and study

Explaining a concept at a different level, generating practice questions, summarising a reading, acting as a patient tutor that never gets bored of the same question. This is one of the strongest uses, and one you will use on yourself during this course.

### Marketing and design

First drafts of copy, variations for testing, concept images, social graphics. The volume of *options* is what changes: producing twenty headline variations used to be a morning and is now a minute.

### Research and analysis

Summarising papers, extracting structured data from documents, drafting literature reviews, explaining a field you are new to. This is also where hallucination does the most damage, so verification is not optional.

### Healthcare, law and finance

Real use exists, and it is almost entirely **assistive and supervised**: drafting notes a doctor signs off, finding relevant precedent a lawyer reads, summarising filings an analyst checks. In these fields the cost of a confident wrong answer is high enough that nobody sensible removes the human.

## Demonstrate

One concrete example, because generalities are easy.

A university department handles roughly two hundred student enquiries a week by email. Many are the same twenty questions. Before, one administrator spent most of two days a week on them.

What they did: the administrator now pastes each enquiry into a tool with a standing instruction describing the department, the rules, and the tone to use. It drafts a reply. She reads it, corrects it, sends it. Roughly seven in ten need only a small edit.

What changed: two days became half a day. Response time dropped from three days to one.

What did not change: she still reads and sends every single one. The first month, the tool confidently invented a deadline that did not exist. She caught it because she was reading. That is the job now, and it is a real job.

## Practice

Find one published account of an organisation using generative AI, from a news article, a company blog or a case study.

Write down three things:

1. What task is the AI actually doing? Be precise.
2. Where is the human in the process, and what do they check?
3. What is the claimed benefit, and is there a number attached to it or just an adjective?

That third question is worth asking every single time. A great many AI claims dissolve on contact with it.

## What to remember

- Generative AI is most useful where output is a draft, not a decision
- Nearly every successful deployment keeps a human checking the output
- Study and explanation is one of the strongest everyday uses
- Ask what the AI actually does, where the human is, and whether the benefit has a number

lessons.title: What generative AI gets wrong
lessons.description: Six failure modes you will meet repeatedly, starting with hallucination.
lessons.content:
## Learn

You will get far more out of these tools if you know their failure modes before you meet them. There are six that matter.

### Hallucination

The model produces something false, stated with the same confidence as everything true it says. Invented citations, invented dates, invented functions in a library, invented legal cases. This is not a bug that will be patched away; it follows from how the models work, which module 2 explains. It is the single most important limitation in this course.

### Knowledge cutoff

A model learned from text gathered up to a point in time. Ask about something after that and it either says it does not know, or, worse, guesses. Some tools now search the web to fill this gap, which helps but introduces its own problem: the model is now only as good as what it found.

### No real understanding of truth

A model has no mechanism for checking whether a statement is true. It produces what is plausible. Plausible and true overlap heavily, which is why these tools are useful, but they are not the same thing, and the gap is where you get hurt.

### Bias

Models learn from human-produced material and reproduce its patterns, including the unwanted ones. This shows up in which names get associated with which jobs, whose dialect is treated as "correct", and which faces a system generates when you ask for "a doctor".

### Context limits

A model can only consider a certain amount of text at once. Go beyond it and the earliest material falls out of view. In a long conversation the model can genuinely forget what you agreed at the start.

### Non-determinism

Ask the same question twice and you may get two different answers. For creative work this is a feature. For anything that needs to be repeatable it is a serious complication, and it is why you cannot treat these tools as a calculator.

### The one that is not on the list

Notice what is missing: the models are not *lying*. Lying requires knowing the truth and choosing otherwise. There is nothing in these systems that knows. They are producing plausible continuations. Calling it lying makes it sound like something you could tell it to stop doing, and you cannot.

## Demonstrate

Try this yourself, right now, in any AI chat tool. It takes two minutes and it is the most valuable two minutes in this module.

Ask it: *"Give me three peer-reviewed papers on the effect of sleep on memory consolidation, with authors, journal and year."*

Now take each one and search for it. Some will be real. There is a good chance at least one is not: a plausible title, plausible authors, a real journal, and no such paper.

Nothing in the answer marked the fake one. It had the same confident tone as the real ones. That is the lesson, and it is worth having learned it here rather than in a submitted assignment.

> If you cannot verify a factual claim from a generative model, you do not yet know whether it is true. Confidence in the output tells you nothing.

## Practice

Run the demonstration above and record what happened.

Then design a second test of your own aimed at one of the other limitations. Some ideas:

- Ask about an event from the last few weeks to probe the knowledge cutoff
- Paste a long document and ask about its first paragraph to probe context limits
- Ask the identical question in three separate new conversations to probe non-determinism
- Ask it to describe a typical person in a profession, several times, and note the pattern

Write down what you expected, what happened, and what it tells you about when to trust the tool.

## What to remember

- Hallucination is structural, not a passing bug
- Confidence in the output carries no information about correctness
- Models have a knowledge cutoff, a context limit, and no concept of truth
- Bias in the training material shows up in the output
- The same question can give different answers, which matters for anything repeatable

lessons.title: Practice questions and answer key
lessons.description: Seven questions covering the whole module, with a full explanation for each.
lessons.content:
These questions cover the whole of module 1. Answer them before you check, and read the explanation for every one, including the ones you get right.

:::quiz
Q. A system is shown thousands of labelled X-ray images and works out for itself which visual features indicate a fracture. Which description fits best?
- Rule-based AI
+ Machine learning
- Generative AI
- It is not AI at all
= Nobody wrote down what a fracture looks like. The system worked out the rule from labelled examples, which is exactly what machine learning means. It is not generative, because the output is a classification, not new content.

Q. What is the most important practical difference between a rule-based system failing and a machine learning system failing?
- The rule-based system is slower to recover
+ The rule-based system fails loudly, while the learned system produces a confident answer that may be wrong
- The learned system will refuse to answer when it is uncertain
- There is no meaningful difference
= A rule-based system given something outside its rules errors or returns nothing, so you know. A learned system still produces output, with no signal that it is out of its depth. This is the source of most unpleasant surprises with AI.

Q. Which of these is generative AI rather than traditional AI?
- Predicting which customers will cancel their subscription
- Flagging a card transaction as likely fraud
+ Drafting a reply to a customer complaint
- Grouping photographs by which person appears in them
= Only the draft reply produces new content. The other three produce a label, a flag or a grouping, which are judgements about things that already exist.

Q. Someone says a language model "lied" to them about a research paper that turned out not to exist. What is the more accurate description?
- The model was trained on false data about that paper
+ The model produced a plausible pattern; it has no mechanism for knowing what is true
- The model deliberately withheld the correct answer
- The model exceeded its context limit
= Lying requires knowing the truth and choosing otherwise. These models produce plausible continuations of text. Plausible and true overlap a great deal, which is why they are useful, but nothing in the system checks the difference.

Q. Which of the five kinds of generative output is currently the least reliable?
- Text
- Code
- Images
+ Video
= Video generation is the newest of the five and quality varies enormously between attempts. Text and code are the most mature. This is a statement about today, and it is the kind of claim worth rechecking rather than trusting a course to keep current.

Q. You are using an AI assistant in a long conversation and it seems to have forgotten a constraint you set at the beginning. What is the most likely explanation?
- The model was retrained during your conversation
- You encountered a knowledge cutoff
+ The conversation exceeded the context window, so the earliest material is no longer in view
- The model is non-deterministic
= A model can only consider a certain amount of text at once. In a long conversation the earliest turns fall out of that window. Non-determinism explains different answers to the same question, not forgetting, and a knowledge cutoff is about training data, not the current conversation.

Q. What is the most reliable way to work with a generative model on factual material?
- Ask it to confirm whether it is certain
- Ask the same question several times and take the most common answer
+ Treat the output as a draft and verify every factual claim independently
- Use the most recent model available
= Asking a model about its own certainty just generates more plausible text. Repeating the question surfaces non-determinism but does not establish truth. Independent verification is the only thing that actually works, which is why every module in this course keeps a human in the loop.
:::

## How to read your score

Five or more correct means you are ready for module 2. Fewer than five is not a problem: go back to the lesson covering what you missed, since module 2 builds directly on these ideas.

lessons.title: Hands-on lab: your first generative AI session
lessons.description: Thirty minutes with a tool open, seeing the strengths and the failure modes yourself.
lessons.content:
This lab takes about thirty minutes. The goal is not to produce anything impressive. It is to see the behaviours from lesson 6 with your own eyes, in one sitting, so that you recognise them for the rest of the course.

## Before you start

Open any general-purpose AI chat tool. ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot and Claude all work for this lab, and each has offered a free tier. Check what the tool you pick currently offers, since features and limits change regularly.

Keep a document open beside it. You will record what happens.

## Step 1: A task it is good at

Ask it to do something with a clear shape and no facts to get wrong.

> Write a polite three-sentence email declining an invitation to speak at an event because of a scheduling conflict. Warm but brief.

Record the output. Ask yourself: would you send this with minor edits? Most people find they would.

## Step 2: The same task, with constraints

Now add constraints, and notice how much the output improves.

> Rewrite that email. I am a final-year engineering student, the event is a college tech fest, and I want to suggest a friend instead. Keep it under sixty words, no exclamation marks.

Record the second output. Compare. This is your first look at why module 4 spends an entire module on prompting.

## Step 3: A task it is bad at

Ask for specific, checkable facts.

> Give me three peer-reviewed papers on the effect of sleep on memory consolidation, with authors, journal and year.

Now verify each one. Search for the exact title. Record, for each of the three, whether you could find it.

## Step 4: Probe a limit of your choosing

Pick one and run it:

- Ask about something that happened in the last few weeks
- Start three separate new conversations and ask the identical question in each, then compare
- Ask it to describe a typical person in a named profession, three times, and note any pattern

Record what you expected and what happened.

## Step 5: Write it up

Four short paragraphs, no more than three hundred words total:

1. One thing it did better than you expected
2. One thing it did worse than you expected
3. One task from your own study or work you would now trust it with, and why
4. One task you would not trust it with, and why

:::hint I am stuck on the fourth paragraph
Look back at the Practice exercise from lesson 3, where you split a task into judgements and production. Anything on the judgement side is a good candidate, especially if being wrong would be costly and hard to notice.
:::

## What good looks like

A strong write-up is specific. "It was good at writing" is weak. "It produced a usable decline email in one attempt, but needed the constraints in step 2 before the tone matched how I actually write" is strong.

A strong write-up is also honest about step 3. If all three papers were real, say so; that happens, and it does not mean hallucination is not a problem. If two were invented, say that too.

lessons.title: Assignment: an honest AI audit
lessons.description: Audit a real process you know well, with a published marking rubric.
lessons.content:
## The task

Produce a short **AI audit** of one real process you know well: something from your studies, your job, a society or club you run, or a family responsibility.

Pick something you actually understand end to end. A process you have only read about will produce a vague audit.

## What to submit

One document, roughly eight hundred to twelve hundred words, with these five sections.

### 1. The process as it is today

Describe it in steps. Who does what, in what order, and roughly how long each step takes. Be concrete enough that a stranger could follow it.

### 2. Where generative AI could help

For each step you identify, state which of the five kinds of generation applies, text, image, audio, video or code, and what specifically it would produce. Not "AI could help with the emails" but "AI drafts the reply to routine membership questions, which I edit before sending".

### 3. Where it should not be used

At least two steps, with a reason for each. Draw on lesson 6. Good reasons include: the cost of a confident wrong answer is high, the step is a judgement rather than production, the material is confidential, or a person is accountable for the outcome.

### 4. The human checkpoints

For every place you proposed AI in section 2, say who checks the output, what specifically they are checking for, and what happens when it is wrong. An audit with no checkpoints is not finished.

### 5. An honest estimate

How much time would this realistically save, and what is the risk you are accepting in exchange? Give a number and say how you arrived at it. "It would save a lot of time" scores nothing.

## Rubric

Marked out of 100.

**Process description, 15 marks.** Full marks for a step-by-step account specific enough for a stranger to follow. Half marks for a general description. Few marks for a single paragraph of summary.

**Identifying opportunities, 25 marks.** Full marks where each proposal names a specific step, the kind of generation, and the concrete output. Marks are lost for vague proposals, and for proposing AI where the step is plainly a judgement.

**Identifying what to avoid, 20 marks.** Full marks for at least two well-reasoned exclusions that connect to a specific limitation from lesson 6. Marks are lost for exclusions with no reason, or reasons that amount to "AI is not good at this".

**Human checkpoints, 25 marks.** Full marks where every proposed use has a named checker, a specific thing being checked, and a stated consequence of failure. This section carries the most weight on purpose: it is the difference between an audit and a wish list.

**Honest estimate, 15 marks.** Full marks for a number with a stated basis and a named risk accepted. Marks are lost for adjectives without numbers, and for claiming a benefit with no corresponding risk.

## Two things that will cost you marks

**Using AI to write the audit without saying so.** You are welcome to use it; this is a course about using it. But say where you used it and what you changed. An audit about human oversight that was itself never overseen is an easy way to lose marks in the checkpoints section.

**Proposing AI for everything.** The strongest submissions are usually the ones that find two or three genuinely good uses and are clear about why the rest of the process should stay as it is.

:::hint I cannot think of a process to audit
Some that have worked well: how your department handles student queries; how your team writes a weekly status report; how a college society plans and promotes an event; how you personally revise for an exam; how a small shop handles stock and reordering; how a family manages a shared calendar and bills.
:::
